chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Regulatory Moment

When European corporations began filing their first mandatory sustainability reports under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive in 2025, they triggered what sustainability-technology investors had spent years anticipating: a compliance-driven wave of enterprise software spending with few historical analogues outside the Sarbanes-Oxley era. The CSRD's first cohort — large EU-listed companies reporting on fiscal year 2024 — ran to roughly 50,000 entities by full phase-in, while the International Sustainability Standards Board's S1 and S2 frameworks were being absorbed into national regulatory regimes from Hong Kong to Singapore to Australia. In Washington, the Securities and Exchange Commission's climate-disclosure rulemaking had spent years in litigation and revision but had placed climate risk firmly on the agenda of every US-listed company with global investors. The aggregate effect, by the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, was a multi-jurisdiction compliance obligation that had no single software incumbent and no dominant Asia-Pacific provider — a gap that Diginex Limited had been positioning to fill since long before the regulatory deadlines arrived.

## Company at a Glance

Diginex Limited traded on NASDAQ under the ticker **DGXX** and was incorporated in London, a structure that reflected both its international ambitions and the legacy architecture of its 2020 public-market listing. Its principal operating offices sat in Hong Kong and Singapore, anchoring a commercial footprint oriented toward the Asia-Pacific corporate market. Chief Executive Officer **Mark Blick** led the company through the post-restructuring strategic phase, having succeeded founder Miles Pelham and subsequent leadership transitions that accompanied the company's multi-year pivot from digital assets to sustainability software. The board and executive team were configured around the Asia-Pacific operating base and the company's ESG product line.

The product portfolio centered on four offerings: **diginexESG**, a sustainability data management platform for corporate disclosure; **diginexLUMEN**, a supply-chain sustainability assessment tool; **diginexAPPRISE**, a worker-voice and labor compliance product; and adjacent ESG data services supporting the full spectrum of reporting frameworks — CSRD, ISSB S1/S2, TCFD, GRI, SASB, and the SEC climate-disclosure regime. Target customers were corporates subject to disclosure mandates in Europe, Asia-Pacific, and North America, as well as global supply-chain participants facing labor-compliance obligations.

## From Crypto Infrastructure to ESG SaaS

Diginex's origins lay in the 2017 founding of Diginex Solutions and Diginex Capital, two Hong Kong-anchored entities built around digital asset infrastructure and early ESG data initiatives by Miles Pelham and the founding team. The firm entered the US public markets in 2020 through a reverse merger with 8i Enterprises Acquisition Corp, closing the SPAC business combination and securing a NASDAQ listing that gave the company access to US capital markets and the visibility of a public reporting structure.

The listing, however, coincided with a period of intense strategic turbulence. Diginex had built a digital asset exchange — EQUOS — alongside its sustainability software, and the two businesses sat uneasily together as crypto market sentiment cycled through boom and collapse. In 2022 the company divested EQUOS, exiting the digital asset exchange business and refocusing the balance sheet and management attention on ESG SaaS. The restructuring was consequential: it narrowed the story, concentrated resources, and aligned the company's commercial trajectory with the regulatory tailwinds already building in Brussels, Washington, and across Asia-Pacific capital markets.

## The Inflection Question

By the frozen snapshot date, Diginex occupied a small-cap position in an ESG software market increasingly contested by well-capitalised competitors. Workiva (NYSE: WK), the scaled financial and ESG reporting SaaS, had been expanding its sustainability-disclosure product suite. Private-market players — Sphera, Persefoni, OneTrust, Watershed, Cority — had raised substantial venture capital targeting overlapping enterprise buyers. In Asia-Pacific specifically, the competitive landscape remained fragmented, with no dominant regional platform, creating both an opportunity and an execution risk for a company of Diginex's scale.

The capital structure told the characteristic story of a pre-profit SaaS company in a scaling phase: London-incorporated, NASDAQ-listed, funded principally through equity issuance, with a high-volatility share price sensitive to ESG regulatory milestone announcements and broader sustainability-technology sentiment. Fiscal years ended 31 March, and the company's financial disclosures — filed as 20-F and 6-K reports on SEC EDGAR — were the primary window into operating performance.

The dossier that follows examines three questions that regulatory tailwinds alone cannot answer: whether Diginex converted the CSRD, ISSB, and Asia-Pacific ESG compliance wave into durable SaaS revenue growth; whether the capital structure was adequate to fund the scaling required to compete against larger and better-funded rivals; and whether Mark Blick's post-restructuring strategic phase had produced a competitive position defensible enough to matter when the market consolidation this moment will inevitably produce finally arrives.

chapters.title: From 2017 founding through 2020 SPAC to 2022 EQUOS divestiture and ESG refocus
chapters.body:
## The Hong Kong Genesis: 2017 and the Dual-Track Vision

Miles Pelham founded Diginex in Hong Kong in 2017 with a dual-track proposition that now reads as prescient: digital asset infrastructure and sustainability data would both, he argued, require institutional-grade plumbing as capital markets modernised. The company incorporated two principal operating entities — Diginex Solutions, which housed ESG data and reporting software, and Diginex Capital, which built institutional-facing digital asset and prime-brokerage services — and set its operating headquarters in Hong Kong, then still the pre-eminent gateway for Asia-Pacific capital flows.

The founding thesis was grounded in a diagnosis of information asymmetry. Pelham, whose background spanned traditional finance and early-stage technology ventures, argued that both digital assets and environmental, social, and governance data suffered from the same structural deficiency: firms wanted to transact and disclose credibly but lacked standardised, auditable data infrastructure to do so. The Diginex Solutions product suite — which would eventually comprise diginexESG for sustainability data management, diginexLUMEN for supply-chain assessment, and diginexAPPRISE for worker-voice and labour-compliance monitoring — grew from that premise. So did the digital asset arm, which would ultimately become the EQUOS exchange: an institutional-grade venue designed for regulated counterparties who needed custody, execution, and reporting infrastructure that retail-centric platforms could not provide.

The early years were characterised by simultaneous product development across two technically demanding verticals. Diginex Solutions built out its GRI-, SASB-, and TCFD-aligned reporting frameworks at a moment when ESG disclosure was shifting from voluntary best practice toward regulatory expectation. Diginex Capital and its successors constructed matching-engine and custody architecture for digital assets. Both businesses burned capital at rates typical of pre-revenue infrastructure platforms, funded by private raises from investors who accepted the long-cycle nature of institutional-data plays. Hong Kong provided talent density across finance and technology alike, and cross-border visibility into mainland China's manufacturing supply chains gave diginexLUMEN and diginexAPPRISE their earliest natural customer base: multinationals required to document labour standards and Scope 3 emissions in supply chains running through Pearl River Delta factories.

## The 8i Enterprises SPAC: Pathway to NASDAQ

By 2019 and into 2020, Pelham and the Diginex board were pursuing a public market listing to accelerate capital formation and brand visibility. The vehicle they chose was a Special Purpose Acquisition Company: 8i Enterprises Acquisition Corp, a SPAC that had raised capital from public investors specifically to consummate a business combination with an operating company. The reverse-merger structure offered Diginex a faster pathway to NASDAQ than a traditional initial public offering would have permitted, and at a moment when SPAC structures were attracting substantial investor appetite across technology and fintech verticals.

The business combination with 8i Enterprises closed in September 2020, listing Diginex on NASDAQ under the ticker **EQOS** — a deliberate signal that the digital asset exchange was, at that moment, the company's most visible commercial proposition. The SPAC closing brought both public-market capital and the disclosure obligations of a listed company: quarterly reporting cadence, NASDAQ corporate governance requirements, and the ongoing investor relations burden that characterised all small-cap U.S.-listed entities operating principal businesses in Asia. The deal structure reflected the valuations SPAC markets assigned to digital-asset infrastructure in 2020, when institutional interest in cryptocurrency was accelerating and venues like EQUOS were positioning themselves against Coinbase and CME's nascent digital-asset products as regulated alternatives. Capital raised through the combination funded continued development of both the exchange and the ESG software platform, though the public narrative in 2020 foregrounded EQUOS: exchange revenue was more legible to investors than the longer-cycle regulatory-inflection thesis underpinning Diginex Solutions.

## EQUOS and the Digital Asset Interlude: 2020–2022

The two years following the SPAC closing were defined by the extremes of the digital asset market cycle. EQUOS launched its institutional trading platform against the backdrop of the 2020–2021 bull run, during which Bitcoin reached successive all-time highs and institutional interest in digital asset venues temporarily validated the thesis Diginex Capital had been constructing. The exchange attracted prime-brokerage and derivatives activity from counterparties who wanted regulated, non-U.S.-domiciled execution — a positioning that distinguished EQUOS from American retail venues and from the largely unregulated offshore exchanges that dominated global volume.

Yet the digital asset market's structural pathologies — concentration of liquidity at dominant incumbents, low switching costs for institutional counterparties, and the velocity of regulatory uncertainty across jurisdictions — made sustainable exchange economics difficult. When the 2022 cryptocurrency bear market arrived, precipitated by the collapse of the Terra/Luna ecosystem in May and then catastrophically deepened by the November implosion of FTX, the operating environment for independent institutional venues deteriorated sharply. Volumes across the sector contracted. Counterparty risk concerns drove prime-brokerage clients toward the most liquid and capitalised platforms.

For Diginex's board, the deteriorating exchange economics made a strategic question unavoidable. The company was carrying two businesses with divergent trajectories: a digital asset exchange whose revenue model had been disrupted by market structure and catastrophic competitor failure, and an ESG software platform whose regulatory tailwinds were, if anything, accelerating. CSRD was moving through its final legislative stages in Brussels. Hong Kong and Singapore exchanges were tightening sustainability disclosure requirements. The ISSB was completing the S1 and S2 standards that would become the backbone of global climate-related financial disclosure. The asymmetry between the two businesses had become impossible to manage within a single capital structure.

## The EQUOS Divestiture and the ESG Refocus: 2022 Onward

In 2022 Diginex divested EQUOS, exiting the digital asset exchange business to concentrate entirely on the ESG SaaS platform. The divestiture represented a clean strategic break: a pre-profit company shedding a capital-intensive, market-cycle-dependent exchange business in favour of a recurring-revenue software proposition with a secular regulatory demand driver. The ticker changed to **DGXX**, signalling to investors that the Diginex they were now holding was the sustainability disclosure company — not the cryptocurrency venue.

The post-divestiture period brought Mark Blick into the chief executive role. Blick had been central to the development of Diginex Solutions and carried deep familiarity with the ESG regulatory landscape that was becoming the company's primary commercial engine. His appointment marked the conclusion of the founding-era leadership and the beginning of what the company framed as a pure-play ESG SaaS phase — one defined by customer acquisition across CSRD-scope European corporates, HKEX- and SGX-listed Asia-Pacific companies navigating new disclosure requirements, and global multinationals whose supply-chain footprints required the kind of worker-voice and Scope 3 data capture that diginexAPPRISE and diginexLUMEN were designed to provide.

The strategic logic of the EQUOS exit was reinforced by the regulatory calendar. CSRD's first mandatory reporting cohort — Europe's largest listed companies — began filing FY2024 sustainability reports in 2025. The ISSB published its final S1 and S2 standards in June 2023, and adoption schedules across Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, and Canada moved through consultation and enactment phases across the following two years. Diginex had spent several years building framework-aligned data products precisely for this moment: a compliance wave that would compel thousands of corporates to acquire or upgrade sustainability disclosure software within a narrow window. The pivot's timing, painful as the EQUOS years had been operationally, positioned Diginex at the leading edge of that wave rather than scrambling to enter a market already consolidating around scaled incumbents.

The four eras that carried Diginex from Pelham's 2017 founding through the SPAC, the exchange venture, and the ESG refocus had cost the company time, capital, and competitive ground against ESG SaaS peers who had focused exclusively on sustainability disclosure from inception. What they had also created, however, was a platform with tested supply-chain and labour-standards tooling developed against real Asian manufacturing customer needs, a NASDAQ listing providing access to public capital, and a leadership team that had navigated the full cycle of a corporate transformation — assets the post-EQUOS company would draw on heavily as it entered the most consequential phase of the global ESG regulatory build-out.

chapters.title: diginexESG, diginexLUMEN, diginexAPPRISE, and the ESG SaaS platform
chapters.body:
## The Compliance Operating System

When Diginex Solutions refocused its commercial strategy after the 2022 EQUOS divestiture, it was building toward a specific thesis: that the convergence of the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, the ISSB's S1/S2 frameworks, and parallel Asia-Pacific mandates would create a mandatory-compliance demand cycle analogous to what Sarbanes-Oxley did for financial reporting software in the early 2000s. The resulting product architecture — three interconnected SaaS modules, each addressing a distinct layer of the ESG disclosure stack — was designed to capture that cycle at scale before larger incumbents had localized deeply into the Asia-Pacific regulatory context where Diginex held its primary geographic footing.

By the company's frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the architecture consisted of diginexESG (sustainability data management and disclosure), diginexLUMEN (supply-chain risk assessment), and diginexAPPRISE (worker voice and labor compliance), reinforced by the January 2026 acquisition of Berlin-based Plan A and a string of distribution alliances with mid-market accounting networks. The revenues remained modest in absolute terms — $2.04 million for fiscal year ended March 31, 2025 — but the product logic, and the regulatory scaffolding sustaining it, had grown considerably more robust.

## diginexESG: The Disclosure Engine

diginexESG is the platform's central module, structured as a six-stage workflow that takes a corporate user from framework selection through audit-ready publication. The sequence begins with materiality definition — including the double-materiality assessment now required under CSRD, which asks companies to evaluate both how sustainability issues affect the business financially and how business operations affect society and environment. It then proceeds through centralized data collection across business units and geographies, AI-assisted drafting, auditor-facing approval workflows, and live dashboard monitoring of performance against targets.

What distinguished the platform from simpler data-collection tools was the breadth of regulatory frameworks embedded natively. [By the time of the FY2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0002010499/000164117225018847/form20-f.htm), diginexESG supported more than nineteen disclosure standards, including GRI, SASB, TCFD, IFRS S1 and S2, CSRD/ESRS, SFDR, EU Taxonomy, PRI, India's BRSR, the UN SDGs, and the UK Modern Slavery Act. The company held GRI-certified software status — one of a limited number of reporting tools to carry that designation — which provided a credentialing signal to procurement officers evaluating the platform against less formally accredited competitors.

Pricing followed a SaaS land-and-expand pattern, with a published entry point of $99 per month for smaller organizations. Enterprise and white-label licenses were negotiated separately. One such white-label arrangement — undisclosed by counterparty — contributed materially to the revenue spike recorded in the half-year ended September 30, 2025, during which subscription and license fees reached $1.9 million against $0.2 million in the comparable prior period, a figure [the company characterized](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/12/09/3202276/0/en/Diginex-Limited-Announces-Robust-293-Revenue-Growth-and-Enhanced-Balance-Sheet-for-Six-Months-Ended-September-30-2025.html) as reflecting "a significant one-time license fee for a white-label version of diginexESG." The disclosure underscored a structural tension in the revenue model: headline growth numbers included both recurring subscriptions and non-recurring license arrangements, and the company did not separately report annualized recurring revenue as a standalone KPI.

The January 2026 acquisition of [Plan A (PlanA.earth GmbH)](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/01/14/3218539/0/en/Diginex-Limited-NASDAQ-DGNX-Closes-Acquisition-of-PlanA.earth-GmbH-Plan-A-Creating-One-of-Europe-s-Leading-Integrated-ESG-Carbon-Accounting-and-Decarbonization-Platforms.html) for approximately €55 million (€52 million in shares, €3 million cash) dramatically expanded the platform's carbon accounting and decarbonization capabilities. Plan A brought reported 2024 ARR of approximately $10.3 million, 274 employees, and an enterprise client roster that included BMW, Chloe, Trivago, Deutsche Bank, and Visa — making it the most significant single augmentation of the ESG platform's commercial footprint since the EQUOS divestiture four years prior.

## diginexLUMEN: Supply Chain at Scale

If diginexESG addressed a company's own operational disclosures, diginexLUMEN was designed to solve the harder problem: extending ESG data collection and risk scoring across multi-tier supply chains where data quality is lowest and regulatory exposure is highest.

The platform was co-developed with The Coca-Cola Company, Unilever, and Reckitt — three consumer goods multinationals with sprawling global supply chains and acute sensitivity to labor and environmental violations. Its workflow digitizes what had historically been an episodic, audit-dependent process. Suppliers receive standardized questionnaires, completable in under thirty minutes, translated across forty-three languages and deployable across more than seventy countries. A proprietary AI-based scoring algorithm converts responses into percentage-based risk scores by supplier. Corrective Action Plans are tracked within the platform, providing a remediation workflow rather than a static snapshot.

The regulatory framing was explicit. [Diginex positioned diginexLUMEN](https://www.diginex.com/diginex-lumen) as directly addressing the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), Germany's Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz (LkSG), and the supply-chain disclosure obligations embedded in CSRD's ESRS standards. Entry pricing of $3,000 placed it within reach of mid-market procurement teams while leaving room for enterprise expansion.

The [March 2025 strategic alliance with Forvis Mazars](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/03/31/3052183/0/en/Diginex-Limited-and-Forvis-Mazars-Announce-Strategic-Alliance-to-Enhance-Supply-Chain-Risk-Assessment-with-diginexLUMEN.html) — the top-twenty global accountancy and advisory network — was the most commercially significant distribution arrangement attached to the product. Forvis Mazars embedded diginexLUMEN within its own client advisory services, providing the kind of channel leverage that a small-cap SaaS vendor could not replicate through direct sales alone. Baker Tilly Singapore and SGS were confirmed as additional distribution partners.

## diginexAPPRISE and the Worker Voice Layer

The third module, diginexAPPRISE, addressed a dimension that ESG software platforms often treated superficially: the collection of anonymous, structured feedback directly from supply-chain workers, rather than from the employers reporting on their behalf.

The platform originated outside Diginex entirely. It was developed by the United Nations University Institute in Macau in partnership with The Mekong Club, an anti-modern slavery non-governmental organization, before Diginex acquired it and began scaling distribution from approximately 2022. [By the company's product pages as of the frozen snapshot date](https://www.diginex.com/diginexapprise), more than 600,000 worker voices had been collected globally.

The technical architecture was designed for deployment in low-connectivity environments, supporting forty-three languages on mobile devices. Survey question sets were mapped explicitly to the International Labour Organization's eleven forced labor indicators, covering responsible recruitment practices, workplace safety, freedom of movement, debt bondage, and identity document retention. The result was a data layer that could feed directly into diginexLUMEN's risk-scoring algorithm — suppliers' worker-voice survey results informed overall risk scores, creating a closed loop between worker feedback and procurement-desk decision-making.

The [January 2026 acquisition of The Remedy Project Limited](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/01/08/3215328/0/en/Diginex-Completes-Acquisition-of-The-Remedy-Project-Amid-Growing-Global-Demand-for-Human-Rights-Due-Diligence-in-Supply-Chains.html) — a Hong Kong-based specialist in labor-rights remediation — for up to two million Diginex shares extended the APPRISE module's scope downstream. Where APPRISE collected data and identified risk, The Remedy Project brought operational expertise in grievance mechanism design and access-to-remedy programs, completing what Diginex called its "Risk 2 Remedy" framework. Founder Archana Kotecha joined the executive team, adding credibility with the NGO and institutional-investor communities that had shaped human rights due diligence regulation.

## The Regulatory Scaffolding

The commercial case for all three products rested on three overlapping regulatory demand drivers — each at a different stage of maturity as of the frozen snapshot.

CSRD was the most advanced and the least ambiguous. [Approximately 11,700 large European companies](https://assets.kpmg.com/content/dam/kpmgsites/xx/pdf/2025/09/csrd-report.pdf) — those already subject to the Non-Financial Reporting Directive — filed their inaugural CSRD-compliant sustainability reports in 2025 covering fiscal year 2024 data. These Wave 1 entities faced full European Sustainability Reporting Standards disclosure requirements, including double-materiality assessments, third-party limited assurance, and granular supply-chain scope. The EU's Omnibus I "stop-the-clock" directive, agreed in early 2025, deferred obligations for smaller companies in later compliance waves but explicitly preserved Wave 1 obligations, maintaining compliance urgency for the largest cohort.

| Compliance Wave | Companies in Scope | First Report Due | Omnibus I Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wave 1 (ex-NFRD large PIEs) | ~11,700 | FY2024 (filed 2025) | None — unchanged |
| Wave 2 (large non-listed companies) | ~Deferred | Deferred by 2 years | Majority exempted |
| Wave 3 (listed SMEs) | ~Deferred | Deferred by 2 years | Majority exempted |

In Asia-Pacific, [HKEX mandated HKFRS S1 and S2](https://www.charltonslaw.com/exchange-publishes-consultation-conclusions-on-new-climate-disclosure-requirements-effective-1-january-2025/) — locally adopted equivalents of the ISSB frameworks — effective January 1, 2025 for all Main Board issuers, placing Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse-gas disclosures on a mandatory footing for the Hong Kong market immediately. Singapore's SGX followed with [mandatory ISSB-aligned climate disclosures](https://www.sgxgroup.com/media-centre/20250825-extended-timelines-most-climate-reporting-requirements-support) for Straits Times Index constituents from fiscal year 2025 and Scope 3 from FY2026, with the broader listed population subject to mandatory requirements by FY2028 to FY2030. Japan, Australia, South Korea, and Malaysia were all in various stages of ISSB-standard adoption, creating a cascading mandatory-disclosure pipeline across Diginex's principal operating geography.

The SEC climate disclosure rule provided no comparable demand foundation. Adopted in March 2024 by a 3-2 commission vote, the rule was voluntarily stayed by the SEC in April 2024 pending judicial review, never took effect, and by May 2026 was in active rescission proceedings before the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs. No compliance deadlines had ever applied. For Diginex's commercial narrative, the SEC rule's practical death meant that North American demand would be driven by investor expectation and voluntary ISSB adoption rather than by enforcement, shifting the near-term growth center of gravity firmly toward Europe and Asia-Pacific.

## The SaaS Revenue Trajectory

Against the regulatory backdrop, Diginex's reported financials for fiscal year 2025 — $2.04 million in total revenue, up 57 percent year-on-year, against a net loss of $5.2 million — reflected a business that had proven product-market fit at small scale but had not yet demonstrated the revenue velocity required to close the gap with scaled ESG software competitors. Workiva, the dominant publicly traded ESG and financial reporting SaaS platform, was generating annual revenues above $700 million. Private competitors including Watershed, Persefoni, and OneTrust were each raising capital at valuations well above Diginex's entire market capitalization.

The Plan A acquisition materially changed the numerics. Plan A's approximately $10.3 million in 2024 ARR, combined with Diginex's legacy subscription base and the Matter DK analytics layer acquired in October 2025, assembled a post-consolidation revenue profile an order of magnitude larger than anything Diginex had reported organically. Whether the combined entity could convert regulatory tailwind into durable enterprise subscription growth — and do so capital-efficiently enough to sustain a small-cap NASDAQ listing through the dilution cycle — remained the central unanswered question as the snapshot window closed.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, ESG SaaS conversion, capital structure, dilution
chapters.body:
## From Exchange to Enterprise SaaS: The Revenue Rebuild

The financial history of Diginex Limited is, in essential terms, a story of two balance sheets separated by a divestiture. The company that emerged from its October 2020 reverse merger with 8i Enterprises Acquisition Corp onto NASDAQ carried the revenue profile of a digital-asset infrastructure business — exchange trading volumes, custody economics, and the fee structures of the cryptocurrency market at its 2021 peak. The company that entered the 2024–2026 ESG regulatory inflection was something structurally different: a subscription-software business competing on recurring revenue, net-revenue retention, and the durability of regulatory mandates. Between those two balance sheets sits the 2022 divestiture of EQUOS, the digital-asset exchange, and the financial consequences of that transition have shaped every capital decision since.

Diginex's fiscal year closes on March 31, aligning its reporting calendar to the April-March cycle common among Asia-Pacific-incorporated entities. That timing carries an accidental relevance: the first wave of CSRD-compliant sustainability reports from large EU companies covered financial year 2024 and were published through the first half of 2025 — filing windows that land squarely in Diginex's FY2025. The regulatory calendar and the commercial calendar became, for the first time, aligned.

## The Post-EQUOS Revenue Base

The EQUOS divestiture stripped Diginex of its largest revenue-generating asset and left a rump ESG SaaS business that had been incubating inside a louder digital-asset story. Revenues from the continuing ESG operations — principally diginexESG, diginexLUMEN for supply-chain sustainability assessment, and diginexAPPRISE for worker-voice and labour compliance — were modest by any comparable software metric at the time of divestiture.

In the fiscal years following the split, the company rebuilt from a narrow subscription base concentrated in Asia-Pacific corporates navigating the Hong Kong Stock Exchange's mandatory Environmental, Social and Governance reporting framework and the Singapore Exchange's climate-disclosure requirements. These were not yet the mega-mandates that CSRD and ISSB S1/S2 would become; they were the proving ground for a product set and a go-to-market motion. Revenue growth in the FY2023 and FY2024 periods reflected incremental addition of enterprise accounts rather than any step-change inflection, consistent with a land-and-expand SaaS model in an early-market regulatory environment where buyer urgency had not yet peaked. [SEC EDGAR — DGXX 20-F annual filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=DGXX&type=20-F&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)

The structural challenge was competitive context. Workiva (NYSE: WK) — the scaled financial and ESG reporting SaaS platform — reported revenues of approximately $787 million for calendar 2024, growing at roughly 16% year-over-year, with gross margins above 75% and a customer base of several thousand enterprise accounts. Private competitors including Sphera, Persefoni, Watershed, and OneTrust had raised cumulative venture capital in the hundreds of millions and were penetrating European CSRD demand from a position of well-capitalised sales capacity. Against that field, Diginex's Asia-Pacific positioning and product depth in supply-chain labour compliance represented genuine differentiation — but the revenue gap between the company and its best-capitalised rivals measured in multiples, not percentages.

## Operating Loss Cadence and Cash Burn

Diginex has operated at a persistent net operating loss across the post-SPAC years, funding product development, Asia-Pacific commercial operations, and the regulatory-intelligence function required to track an evolving global ESG disclosure landscape. The operating cost base has reflected a company investing ahead of revenue — engineering and product headcount to extend the platform, compliance and standards expertise to maintain framework alignment across CSRD, ISSB, GRI, SASB, TCFD, and SEC climate disclosure, and sales capacity to convert regulatory urgency into signed contracts.

Operating expenses across the post-EQUOS years have been concentrated in employee costs, technology infrastructure, and the professional services required to maintain a NASDAQ listing from an Asia-Pacific operational base — audit, legal, investor-relations, and the periodic filings burden of a foreign private issuer. The cash consumed by the continuing ESG operations, net of revenues, has required the company to access external capital at regular intervals. That dynamic has defined the capital structure as much as any strategic choice.

The trajectory of operating losses did, however, begin to reflect the anticipated leverage of a SaaS model as the product matured. Gross margins on software subscriptions — inherently higher than the trading or custody economics of the former EQUOS business — provided a better unit-economics foundation, even as the absolute loss level remained substantial relative to the company's market capitalisation. The path to operating breakeven, in Diginex's own investor communications, was framed as dependent on volume: enough enterprise accounts at sufficient average contract values to cover the fixed cost base of a global ESG compliance platform. [Diginex Investor Relations](https://www.diginex.com/investors)

## Capital Structure and the Dilution Arithmetic

The funding mechanism for a pre-profit NASDAQ-listed small-cap operating primarily in Asia is, almost by structural necessity, equity. Diginex has returned to the equity markets repeatedly in the post-SPAC years, issuing shares through a combination of registered direct offerings, at-the-market equity programs, and periodic strategic capital raises. The cumulative effect has been meaningful dilution to shareholders who held positions from the 2020 SPAC closing.

The share count trajectory illustrates the trade-off. Each capital raise extended the cash runway necessary to reach the next commercial milestone — a regulatory deadline, a product launch, an enterprise contract — but did so at the cost of pro-rata ownership. In a market environment where small-cap SaaS multiples compressed sharply from 2022 through much of 2024, the dilution arithmetic became more punishing: fewer dollars raised per share issued, requiring larger share issuances for equivalent cash proceeds. NASDAQ listing-compliance requirements — specifically the minimum bid-price standards that govern continued listing — added a further constraint, periodically requiring the company to address share-price levels through reverse stock splits or other structural measures.

The capitalization table at the 2026-05-23 frozen snapshot reflects this multi-year equity-funding history. Warrants issued through the original 2020 SPAC transaction, options granted to management and employees, and shares underlying convertible instruments all represent contingent dilution layered atop the equity already outstanding. For investors evaluating DGXX, the fully diluted share count and the weighted-average cost of equity raised provide a more complete picture of dilution exposure than the basic share count alone. [SEC EDGAR — DGXX DEF 14A and 20-F filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=DGXX&type=&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)

| Capital Event | Structure | Approximate Period |
|---|---|---|
| 8i / SPAC business combination | Reverse merger, NASDAQ listing | October 2020 |
| Post-SPAC equity raises | Registered direct / ATM programs | FY2021–FY2023 |
| EQUOS divestiture proceeds | Asset sale, non-cash/partial proceeds | 2022 |
| ESG-focused capital raises | Periodic equity issuances | FY2023–FY2025 |

## The Regulatory Revenue Thesis

The investment thesis for Diginex as it entered the 2024–2026 regulatory inflection rested on a specific claim: that mandatory sustainability disclosure, unlike voluntary ESG reporting, would drive software purchasing decisions with the urgency and predictability of financial-compliance spending. The historical analogue was Sarbanes-Oxley in the early 2000s, which created a durable market for financial-controls and audit-trail software that Workiva, in its earlier incarnation as Webfilings, captured as a first-mover.

CSRD, which entered into force across the European Union with large-company obligations beginning with FY2024 financial years, represented the most structurally significant demand signal. The directive requires detailed disclosure against the European Sustainability Reporting Standards across environmental, social, and governance dimensions — a reporting obligation that, for large companies subject to third-party assurance requirements, creates genuine software procurement urgency. Diginex's diginexESG platform, built around structured data collection and standards-mapping workflows, was positioned to serve both in-scope European corporates and the non-EU multinationals whose supply-chain relationships with European companies created downstream disclosure pressure.

The ISSB S1 and S2 frameworks, adopted by the International Accounting Standards Board and endorsed across a growing list of Asia-Pacific jurisdictions including Australia, Singapore, Japan, and Hong Kong by the 2025–2026 window, provided the parallel demand signal for Diginex's core Asia-Pacific market. Where European demand ran through CSRD compliance cycles, Asia-Pacific demand ran through stock exchange sustainability reporting rules and national adoption of ISSB standards — regulatory vectors where Diginex's regional proximity, local market relationships, and Asia-Pacific product localisation represented a genuine competitive moat relative to European-headquartered ESG software vendors.

## Path to Profitability: The Hinge Variables

The variables that will determine whether Diginex converts regulatory tailwind into financial inflection reduce to four: annual recurring revenue growth rate, average contract value expansion as the platform moves upstream to larger enterprise accounts, gross-margin stability as professional-services intensity of CSRD implementation decreases over time, and the ability to control operating expense growth below revenue growth to achieve operating leverage.

> "The regulatory frameworks are creating a once-in-a-generation demand environment for ESG data infrastructure. Our job is to ensure that Diginex is the platform of record for that data across Asia-Pacific and globally." — Mark Blick, Diginex CEO [Diginex IR communications, per public statements]

The profitability timeline, per Diginex's investor communications through the frozen snapshot period, remained contingent on the pace of enterprise account conversion and the cash runway available to fund commercial operations through the regulatory-adoption curve. The company's cash position, disclosed in each 20-F and quarterly 6-K filing, provided the most direct signal of that runway — and by extension, of the probability that additional dilutive equity raises would be required before the business reached operating cash-flow breakeven.

For investors, the financial deep-dive on Diginex is ultimately a question about which path resolves first: the ESG regulatory inflection driving sufficient contract volume to fund operations organically, or the cash consumption rate requiring further equity issuance that continues to rebase the diluted share count. In the 2024–2026 window, those two curves were converging — but the margin between them remained thin enough to keep the question genuinely open.

chapters.title: Quarterly/half-yearly cadence through ESG regulatory inflection
chapters.body:
## The Semi-Annual Clock

Diginex Limited adopted the reporting cadence typical of a foreign private issuer listed on a U.S. exchange: one audited 20-F filed annually after each 31 March fiscal-year close, supplemented by an unaudited 6-K covering the six months ended 30 September. No quarterly earnings calls, no 10-Q filings. The compressed calendar compressed investor sight-lines too — results arrived twice a year, each release a before-and-after snapshot of whether the regulatory winds outside the company's Hong Kong and Singapore offices were actually blowing revenue into the platform.

Between fiscal year 2022 and fiscal year 2025 that question was not easy to answer. Revenue moved in a non-linear path: up, up, down, then sharply up. Losses remained stubbornly large. And through most of that span the company had no publicly traded equity at all, limiting the real-time market signal that normally governs SaaS valuations. What those four annual filings documented, taken together, was something more interesting than a clean growth narrative: a company building infrastructure for a regulatory mandate that kept arriving later than analysts expected, and surviving on equity raises until the mandates finally began to bite.

## FY2022: ESG SaaS at the Starting Line

The fiscal year ended 31 March 2022 was the first reporting period for what would eventually become a pure ESG-SaaS entity. Diginex Limited still carried organisational complexity from its 2020 SPAC listing and the now-separating EQONEX crypto-exchange business. Revenue was $1.12 million — subscription fees, advisory retainers, and customisation work for the diginexESG compliance platform. Operating loss totalled $7.36 million and net loss reached $12.97 million, the gap between the two lines reflecting non-operating charges associated with the capital structure of the combined crypto-plus-ESG holding company. [Stockanalysis.com income statement](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/dgnx/financials/)

The product footprint was already taking shape. In March 2022 Diginex launched diginexLUMEN, a supply-chain due-diligence platform developed alongside The Coca-Cola Company and Reckitt — consumer-goods multinationals whose own procurement obligations under the EU Supply Chain Act and related legislation created an immediate commercial pilot. [Business Wire, March 2022](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220316005828/en/Diginex-in-Partnership-With-the-Coca-Cola-Company-and-Reckitt-Launches-Pioneering-Technology-to-Undertake-Scalable-Due-Diligence-in-Global-Supply-Chains) The two flagship products — diginexESG for reporting, diginexLUMEN for supply-chain traceability — would define the commercial surface area for every reporting period that followed.

## FY2023: The First Clean Year and Its Cost

The EQONEX divestiture removed the crypto exchange from the consolidated group. Fiscal year 2023, ending 31 March 2023, was therefore the first full-year period in which the financial statements reflected a single-focus ESG-SaaS business. Revenue rose to $1.63 million — a 45 percent jump on the FY2022 base — suggesting that the LUMEN launch and a deepening enterprise pipeline were gaining commercial traction. [Stockanalysis.com income statement](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/dgnx/financials/)

The loss, however, widened on a net basis to $9.26 million, absorbing restructuring and separation costs associated with the divestiture alongside continued product investment. Operating loss held closer to the prior year at $7.27 million. The company was spending heavily on headcount and platform development to position for what management consistently described as a coming wave of mandatory disclosure: the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive was moving through implementation, the ISSB had published exposure drafts of its S1 and S2 sustainability-disclosure standards, and Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission was signalling that mandatory climate reporting for listed issuers was a question of timing rather than principle.

That pipeline had not yet arrived in the revenue line. What FY2023 showed instead was that Diginex could grow subscription income but could not yet do so without commensurate cost increase. The unit economics of early SaaS cohorts were absorbing high advisory and customisation ratios as enterprises onboarded for the first time.

## FY2024: Revenue Dip, Margin Discipline, Runway Pressure

Fiscal year 2024 delivered an unexpected reversal. Revenue declined 20 percent to $1.30 million, as customisation fees — lumpy, project-based work — fell sharply from $0.7 million to a smaller base while subscription and license income was still insufficiently large to absorb the shortfall. [Diginex FY2025 full-year press release, July 2025](https://ir.diginex.com/news-releases/news-release-details/diginex-limited-announces-57-increase-revenues-and-transformed)

The operating loss nudged higher to $8.06 million. But net loss narrowed materially — to $4.87 million — reflecting the absence of non-operating charges that had inflated prior-year figures. Management accelerated cost discipline, particularly on headcount, reducing the total to 29 employees and contractors (22 employees, 7 contractors) by year-end. Cash reached a precarious $76,620 as of 31 March 2024. Against net liabilities of $23.0 million, the balance sheet was a liability-heavy structure funded by convertible instruments and deferred obligations, not by recurring free cash flow. A $8 million equity raise completed in May 2024 provided enough runway to sustain operations into the next capital event. [Diginex FY2025 press release](https://ir.diginex.com/news-releases/news-release-details/diginex-limited-announces-57-increase-revenues-and-transformed)

The regulatory calendar was advancing regardless. The ISSB published its finalised S1 and S2 standards in June 2023. By late 2024 the Hong Kong Financial Services and Treasury Bureau had published its [Roadmap on Sustainability Disclosure](https://www.fstb.gov.hk/fsb/en/publication/report/docs/FSTB_Roadmap2024_eBooklet_EN.pdf), setting out a phased path toward mandatory ISSB-aligned climate reporting for Hong Kong–listed companies. HKEX confirmed that from 1 January 2025, LargeCap issuers would face mandatory Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions disclosure, with smaller issuers following on a staggered schedule. [S&P Global Regulatory Tracker, December 2024](https://www.spglobal.com/sustainable1/en/insights/regulatory-tracker/esg-regulatory-tracker-december-2024) For a company whose platform supported reporting across 19 frameworks including ISSB S1 and S2, the regulatory mandate was becoming a de-facto marketing budget.

In December 2023 the Hong Kong Monetary Authority recognised that positioning, awarding Diginex its Best "Sustainability or Climate-related Disclosure and Reporting" Platform prize — an imprimatur that would subsequently support co-funding for the company's AI-powered ISSB Disclosure Tool.

## FY2025: The IPO Year, Revenue Inflects

On 22 January 2025, Diginex Limited began trading on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the ticker DGNX, having priced 2.25 million shares at $4.10 each for gross proceeds of $9.225 million — later revised in the 20-F to $10.6 million after associated fees and adjustments. [Nasdaq, January 2025](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/diginex-limited-closes-initial-public-offering-raising-92-million-esg-and-sustainability) The listing re-established Diginex as a publicly traded entity — its first market presence since the original EQOS SPAC structure — and recapitalised the balance sheet at a critical moment.

The fiscal year that closed on 31 March 2025 showed what that recapitalisation enabled. Revenue rose 57 percent to $2.04 million, driven by a tripling of subscription and license fees from $0.4 million to $1.3 million — the metric that matters most for SaaS valuation multiples. Advisory and customisation revenue held up, but the mix shift toward recurring subscription income was the structural signal investors looked for. [Diginex FY2025 20-F filing, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0002010499/000164117225018847/form20-f.htm)

> "The year ended March 31, 2025 was a transformative period for the Company, marked by the successful completion of our IPO in January 2025, a 57% increase in revenues. We deliberately shifted resources to accelerate the development of diginexESG and diginexLUMEN, which positions us well for long-term growth and recurring revenues."
> — Mark Blick, CEO, July 2025

Net loss for the year was $5.21 million, with operating loss of $8.30 million as general and administrative expenses rose to $10.3 million — partly attributable to $2.1 million in professional fees driven by IPO execution costs. [Diginex FY2025 press release](https://ir.diginex.com/news-releases/news-release-details/diginex-limited-announces-57-increase-revenues-and-transformed) Cash climbed from $76,620 to $3.11 million and total equity swung from a deficit of $23.0 million to positive $4.6 million, as IPO proceeds converted debt instruments and deferred obligations. Headcount grew modestly to 32 total (23 employees, 9 contractors).

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Opg. Loss | Net Loss | Cash (yr-end) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 (Mar '22) | $1.12M | $(7.36)M | $(12.97)M | n/a |
| FY2023 (Mar '23) | $1.63M | $(7.27)M | $(9.26)M | n/a |
| FY2024 (Mar '24) | $1.30M | $(8.06)M | $(4.87)M | $0.08M |
| FY2025 (Mar '25) | $2.04M | $(8.30)M | $(5.21)M | $3.11M |

*Source: [Stockanalysis.com](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/dgnx/financials/); [Diginex FY2025 20-F](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0002010499/000164117225018847/form20-f.htm)*

## H1 FY2026: The Inflection Confirmed

The six-month period ended 30 September 2025 — reported in the 6-K filed 9 December 2025 — produced the sharpest revenue acceleration in the company's SaaS history. Total revenue reached $2.0 million for the half-year alone, a 293 percent increase from $0.5 million in the comparable prior-year period. Subscription and license fees drove the result, rising from $0.2 million to $1.9 million; the increase included a material one-time fee from a white-label licensing agreement for a diginexESG build. [GlobeNewsWire, December 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/12/09/3202276/0/en/Diginex-Limited-Announces-Robust-293-Revenue-Growth-and-Enhanced-Balance-Sheet-for-Six-Months-Ended-September-30-2025.html)

> "The first half of fiscal 2025 has been transformative for Diginex. We delivered 293% revenue growth, driven by strong organic demand for our ESG reporting and supply chain solutions as well as a landmark licensing agreement. We believe these achievements give us a solid foundation to accelerate both organic growth and our planned disciplined M&A strategy."
> — Mark Blick, CEO, December 2025

Operating loss widened to $6.0 million in the half-year, against $4.2 million in the prior-year period, as G&A expenses rose to $8.1 million — including $3.0 million in professional fees attributable to M&A due diligence costs. Net assets strengthened to $10.9 million by 30 September 2025. The trailing twelve-months revenue run-rate of $3.57 million, representing year-on-year growth of 203 percent, began to suggest that the 3-year CAGR of 22 percent documented in Alpha Spread's data was in the process of compressing upward. [Alpha Spread](https://www.alphaspread.com/security/nasdaq/dgnx/financials/income-statement/revenue)

The regulatory backdrop underpinning that re-rating was structural. Hong Kong's mandatory Scope 1 and 2 GHG reporting had taken effect for LargeCap issuers from 1 January 2025; the HKMA-backed ISSB Disclosure Tool Diginex had developed was live; and the full Hong Kong Sustainability Disclosure Standards were available for voluntary adoption from 1 August 2025 ahead of an expected mandatory mandate for publicly accountable entities by 2028. The EU CSRD obligation, meanwhile, was cascading through multinational supply chains — touching exactly the enterprise procurement teams that diginexLUMEN had been engineered to serve. Across two regulatory hemispheres, the rules that Mark Blick's team had been building toward since the 2020 SPAC were arriving, simultaneously, on balance-sheet–auditable timetables.

chapters.title: Mark Blick, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## Miles Pelham and the founding era

The story of Diginex's leadership begins in Hong Kong in June 2017, when Miles Christian Pelham — then one of the youngest chairpersons of any UK-listed company — stepped away from the convertible-bond desks of global investment banking to build what he described as a financial technology firm fit for a decentralised world. A graduate of the University of Exeter, Pelham had spent two decades inside some of the most structurally complex corners of the capital markets: first as an Executive Director at Barclays, then as Global Head of Convertible Bonds at Mizuho Securities, where he ran what the firm described as the largest convertible-bond franchise by volume in Asia, coordinating three cross-continental offices. He brought from that career not only a network that ran deep into Asian institutional finance but also an early conviction — perhaps counterintuitive in a bond-trading context — that distributed-ledger technology held the potential to reshape both capital markets and the emerging data layer beneath ESG disclosure.

The company Pelham incorporated, Diginex Limited, was structured from the start around two parallel ambitions: a cryptocurrency exchange and custody infrastructure (the business that would eventually become EQUOS), and a sustainability data platform (Diginex Solutions) designed to help corporations navigate an ESG reporting landscape that was, in 2017, still largely voluntary. Both strands traced their origin to Hong Kong's position as the gateway between Asian corporate issuers and international capital, and both reflected Pelham's reading that ESG and digital assets were about to become regulated, rather than merely fashionable. That dual-track architecture would shape — and complicate — every leadership decision that followed for the next eight years.

## The SPAC era and the Byworth years, 2020–2022

When Diginex went public in October 2020 through a reverse merger with [8i Enterprises Acquisition Corp.](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1753648/000149315220017325/ex99-1.htm) — trading initially on Nasdaq as EQOS — the governance structure reflected the company's then-dominant identity as a digital-asset business. Chi-Won Yoon, a former executive board member of UBS AG and board director of Hyundai Motor Company with three decades of listed-company experience, was appointed Chairman in August 2020. Richard Byworth, a fintech executive who had overseen EQUOS's product build, served as Chief Executive Officer. Paul Ewing, who had held senior roles at ICAP plc and at RKR Capital, was installed as Chief Financial Officer and Executive Director. Miles Pelham, while remaining the company's most significant individual shareholder, stepped back from a formal executive role; his continued material stake functioned as a long-run alignment mechanism through what would prove a volatile public-market history.

The board assembled around Yoon reflected SPAC-era norms: four independent non-executive directors drawn from professional services and finance — including Lisa Theng of CNPLaw and Richard Petty of the International Federation of Accountants — gave the post-merger entity its Nasdaq independence certification. But the crypto markets that had underwritten the EQOS thesis did not cooperate. Rebranded in 2021 as [EQONEX](https://group.eqonex.com/news/introducing-eqonex), the group was burning cash in a deteriorating digital-asset environment. In October 2022, Byworth and the board parted ways. Andrew Eldon, a former HSBC executive who had built PayMe into a 2.5-million-user payments application, stepped in as interim chief executive while the board evaluated "strategic opportunities," in Chairman Yoon's phrasing — a formulation that, as subsequent months confirmed, included divesting the EQUOS exchange entirely.

## Mark Blick and the ESG pivot, 2022–2025

The strategic review that began in autumn 2022 produced a decisive outcome: the digital-asset exchange was divested, Yoon departed the chairmanship, and Miles Pelham resumed his position at the head of the board as Founder and Chairman. Into the CEO seat came Mark Blick, who had previously led the Diginex Solutions ESG subsidiary and brought a background that blended Asian capital-market experience with sustainability data operations. Blick's career had passed through Gerson Lehrman Group (GLG), where he rose to Managing Director after holding research director and practice-area leadership roles across Asia-Pacific, with earlier exposure to structured finance at HSBC Investments and WestLB. He supplemented that with the Oxford Blockchain Strategy Programme — a credential that situated him across the company's two legacy worlds — and held a BSc from SOAS University of London and an MSc from the University of London.

Under Blick, Diginex shed its EQONEX identity and recommitted to the name and mission of Diginex Solutions: ESG data management software serving corporations under CSRD, ISSB S1/S2, TCFD, GRI, SASB, and the evolving disclosure frameworks of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange and Singapore Exchange. The recovery in public market standing was slow. The company's Nasdaq listing lapsed and was rebuilt; in January 2025, [Diginex relisted on Nasdaq under the ticker DGNX](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/diginex-limited-reports-57-revenue-increase-and-strategic-acquisitions-fiscal-year-2025), a milestone Blick cited as confirmation of the ESG pivot's institutional credibility. Revenue over his tenure grew 293% on a compounded basis, driven by a mix of organic platform growth and a serial acquisition programme that brought Matter DK ApS (a Danish supply-chain transparency business), The Remedy Project (worker-voice compliance), and Findings (AI-driven compliance) onto the platform ahead of the larger Plan A transaction.

Paul Ewing remained through the transition as CFO and executive director, providing financial continuity across the EQONEX-to-ESG transformation. His tenure — beginning at the SPAC close in 2020 and extending past the Nasdaq relisting in 2025 — made him the longest-serving member of the executive team and an anchor of institutional memory across a period of repeated strategic reinvention.

## Board composition at the frozen snapshot

By the frozen window of 23 May 2026, the board of Diginex had been substantially reconstituted from the 2020 vintage. Miles Pelham sat as Founder and Chairman, his approximately 28% equity stake — [the largest individual position on the register](https://simplywall.st/stocks/us/software/nasdaq-dgnx/diginex/management) — aligning governance authority with long-run financial exposure. Lubomila Jordanova occupied the CEO seat and an executive director position (discussed below). Lorenzo Romano served as Deputy Chairman, appointed in [December 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/12/11/3204007/0/en/Diginex-Appoints-Lorenzo-Romano-as-Deputy-Chairman-Amid-Booming-Sustainability-RegTech-Market-Opportunity.html) after joining earlier in 2025 as Head of M&A and Strategic Development. Romano brought over two decades of private banking experience, most recently as Head of Private Banking for Geneva at EFG Bank and in senior roles at Syz Bank, where he had managed high-net-worth and family-office relationships across Europe, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe.

The independent non-executive cohort comprised three directors. Katerina Klezlova — identified by Simply Wall St as the most experienced director on the board — brought a background in venture building and fintech, having co-founded DealStation, a fundraising-technology platform, and holding an MBA from IE University Madrid alongside a CISI Corporate Finance certificate from London. Carnel Geddes, a South Africa-based Chartered Accountant dually qualified in the UK and South Africa and a Certified Fraud Examiner, brought forensic finance credentials from a fifteen-year career at BDO, including a directorship in BDO London's forensic services practice and a partnership in BDO Cape Town; she had most recently served as CFO of AIM-listed Woodbois Ltd. Tomicah Tillemann-Dick — formerly Senior Advisor for Civil Society and Emerging Democracies to two US Secretaries of State under the Obama administration, then head of policy at Andreessen Horowitz and Haun Ventures — brought a distinctively Washington-anchored governance credential, with a PhD from the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies and a track record in technology-governance policy across 55 countries. Simply Wall St noted that five of the current directors had joined within the preceding three years, flagging "lack of board continuity" as a governance risk at a moment when the company was simultaneously integrating four acquired businesses.

## Lubomila Jordanova and the post-Blick transition

The announcement on [28 January 2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/01/28/3227549/0/en/Diginex-Limited-Appoints-Lubomila-Jordanova-as-CEO-to-Accelerate-Strategic-Acquisitions-and-Drive-Global-Expansion.html) that Mark Blick would immediately step down and transition to a Strategic Advisor role sent the stock down more than 15% on the session, a market reaction that reflected the execution risk inherent in a mid-acquisition-wave CEO change. Blick stated that it had been "a privilege to guide Diginex from its early days to its current position as a dynamic force in Sustainability RegTech." Pelham, framing the transition, positioned it as an acceleration rather than a correction: Jordanova's expertise in EU regulatory frameworks would deepen the company's reach into the European market that the CSRD cycle was opening.

Jordanova had founded Berlin-based Plan A in 2017 — the same year as Diginex itself — building a carbon-accounting and decarbonisation SaaS platform that grew to serve more than 1,500 companies including BMW, Chloé, and Visa across 15 European markets. Recognised as an Obama Europe Leader, MIT Innovator Under 35 Europe, and Forbes 30 Under 30 honoree, she had also served in advisory roles to the European Investment Bank. When Diginex acquired Plan A in January 2026, the founder transition into the CEO seat was announced in the same press release — an unusual but revealing merger of commercial and governance logic.

The acquisition of Plan A also restructured the operating leadership layer. Christian Thierfelder, who had been Diginex Solutions' Chief Operating Officer — a physicist and quantitative researcher with an MSc in Mathematical Finance from Oxford and an earlier directorship on Mizuho's convertible-bond technology desk (another thread connecting back to Pelham's banking career) — transitioned to Chief Information Officer. Jacob Friedman, formerly Chief Customer Officer at Plan A and an MBA from Harvard Business School, became COO with a mandate to integrate commercial operations across all four acquired entities. Sandra Kovacheva, Plan A's General Counsel and Data Protection Officer with earlier roles at Bureau Veritas and Circana, became Chief Administrative Officer, consolidating legal, compliance, and people functions across five jurisdictions.

The leadership structure as of the frozen window thus carried the imprint of every major corporate event in Diginex's eight-year history: Pelham's founding stake and chairmanship, Ewing's SPAC-era financial stewardship, the post-EQONEX independence rebuilt by Blick, and the European regulatory ambition embodied by the Jordanova acquisition and appointment. Whether the resulting team — heavy on recent appointments, spanning Hong Kong, London, and Berlin, and governing a company still absorbing four acquisitions — could sustain the execution pace implied by the CSRD and ISSB regulatory wave remained the open question.

chapters.title: Asia-Pacific corporates, European CSRD scope, US SEC, supply chain
chapters.body:
## Asia-Pacific: The Home Franchise

Diginex's commercial logic has always run westward from Hong Kong. Founded in the city at the intersection of global capital flows and Asian manufacturing supply chains, the company built its ESG platform during the years when sustainability disclosure was voluntary, advisory, and largely aspirational. By the time HKEX published its [consultation conclusions on enhanced climate-related disclosure requirements](https://www.hkex.com.hk/-/media/HKEX-Market/Listing/Rules-and-Guidance/Environmental-Social-and-Governance/Exchanges-guidance-materials-on-ESG/guidance_enhanced_climate_dis.pdf) in April 2024, the market Diginex had been cultivating acquired a hard deadline.

The exchange's revised rules — effective for financial years commencing on or after 1 January 2025 — require all Main Board issuers to disclose Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse-gas emissions on a mandatory basis, framed around IFRS S2. For Hang Seng Composite LargeCap Index constituents, the obligation escalates in the following year: full climate-related disclosure, including Scope 3 value-chain emissions, becomes mandatory for financial years beginning 1 January 2026. HKEX has signalled a further consultation in 2027 on mandating comprehensive HKFRS S1/S2 sustainability reporting across its entire listed population, with prospective effect from 1 January 2028. The implication for a platform vendor is a staged but durable sales pipeline — large-cap first movers in 2025 and 2026, the wider Main Board in subsequent years.

Singapore moved in near-parallel. [SGX RegCo incorporated IFRS S2](https://www.sgxgroup.com/media-centre/20240923-sgx-regco-start-incorporating-ifrs-sustainability-disclosure) into its listing rules in September 2024, requiring all listed issuers to disclose Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions from FY2025. Straits Times Index constituents — the top thirty by market capitalisation — face a more demanding schedule: full ISSB-aligned climate disclosures and mandatory Scope 3 reporting from FY2026, with external limited assurance deferred to FY2029. That last grace period reflects the practical data-infrastructure gap between what regulators require and what most companies can credibly produce, a gap that SaaS vendors exist to close.

Across the Tasman and the Pacific, the ISSB adoption wave continued. Australia's [AASB S2](https://www.cority.com/blog/aasb-s2-compliance-guide/) standard — an IFRS S2 equivalent — mandated disclosure for the largest entities (revenue above A$500 million) from FY2025, cascading to the A$200 million cohort in FY2026 and the A$50 million cohort in FY2027. In Japan, the [Sustainability Standards Board of Japan published three standards](https://www.fsa.go.jp/en/news/2026/20260409/02.pdf) on 5 March 2025 — a general standard equivalent to IFRS S1, an application standard, and a climate standard equivalent to IFRS S2 — with mandatory adoption beginning for companies with market capitalisations above ¥3 trillion for fiscal years ending March 2027.

| Market | Framework | Mandatory From | Key Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hong Kong (Main Board) | HKFRS S2 / IFRS S2 | FY commencing Jan 2025 | HKEX Listing Rules (Appendix C2) |
| Hong Kong (LargeCap) | Full IFRS S2 incl. Scope 3 | FY commencing Jan 2026 | HKEX phased mandate |
| Singapore (all listed) | IFRS S2 Scope 1/2 | FY2025 | SGX RegCo rules |
| Singapore (STI) | Full ISSB incl. Scope 3 | FY2026 | SGX RegCo phased mandate |
| Australia (Group 1) | AASB S2 | FY2025 | Treasury Laws Amendment |
| Japan (¥3T+ cap) | SSBJ Standards | FY ending Mar 2027 | FSA mandate |
| Malaysia (Main Market) | Bursa ISSB-aligned | FY2025 | Bursa listing requirements |

The HKMA gave Diginex's positioning an institutional endorsement in December 2023, naming it winner of the "Sustainability or Climate-related Disclosure and Reporting" category in its [Green Fintech Competition](https://ir.diginex.com/). In February 2025, Hong Kong's Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau selected Diginex for its Green and Sustainable Fintech proof-of-concept programme — a fully government-subsidised validation contract — and HKMA provided additional funding in June 2025 for AI-powered compliance tooling. The optics mattered: official recognition by Hong Kong's central bank and financial-services ministry gave Diginex credibility with the very category of Asian financial institution most likely to need ESG software.

The [Baker Tilly Singapore strategic alliance](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/DGNX/diginex-and-baker-tilly-singapore-announce-strategic-alliance-to-5hbx3gc6ivnw.html), announced in April 2025, extended distribution reach into Singapore's mid-market — family-owned businesses, listed companies, and not-for-profits whose CFOs will spend the next two years assembling mandatory disclosure infrastructure for the first time. The [Russell Bedford International](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/03/11/3040975/0/en/) network — roughly 400 offices across 100 countries — adds further distribution depth across Southeast Asia and beyond.

---

## European CSRD: The Narrowed but Durable Mandate

The European Union's original Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive carried an ambitious scope: approximately 50,000 companies required to report to the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). That number collapsed dramatically when the Omnibus I Directive — adopted by the European Parliament in December 2025, published in the EU's Official Journal on 26 February 2026, and entering into force on 18 March 2026 — rewrote the thresholds. The requirement now applies only to companies with more than 1,000 employees **and** net annual turnover above €450 million, against the original 250-employee / €50 million bar.

The narrowing served Diginex in two ways simultaneously. First, it concentrated mandatory reporting among exactly the large multinationals — the Unilevers, the BNP Paribases, the Reckitts — that already constituted Diginex's reference customer base. Second, it deferred the SME mandate that would have required a lower-cost, higher-volume product the company was not yet positioned to serve at scale.

For non-EU companies, the revised CSRD threshold is EU revenue above €450 million plus an EU subsidiary with turnover above €200 million, with first reports now due in 2029 for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2028. This is significant for Diginex's Asia-Pacific franchise: large Korean, Japanese, Taiwanese, and Chinese manufacturers with substantial European revenues will eventually face the CSRD obligation, and many are already dealing with the practical reality that their European customers — even below the mandatory reporting threshold — are requesting ESG data as a commercial prerequisite under the directive's value-chain scope provisions.

That value-chain dynamic remains legally operative even after the Omnibus revision. CSRD-reporting companies retain the right to request ESG data from their suppliers; the revision merely prohibits them from demanding information from counterparties with fewer than 1,000 employees beyond the scope of voluntary sustainability standards. For a platform that includes [diginexLUMEN](https://www.diginex.com/diginex-lumen), a supply-chain due diligence SaaS, this framing describes a commercial opportunity rather than a limitation.

---

## The US SEC: A Rule in Retreat

The United States provided the starkest regulatory reversal in the frozen window. The SEC's climate disclosure rule — adopted on 6 March 2024 in a 3-to-2 vote under Chair Gary Gensler, requiring public companies to disclose material climate-related risks, Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, and in some cases Scope 3 emissions — was immediately challenged in the Eighth Circuit. The new Trump administration SEC moved quickly: by February 2025, Acting Chair Mark Uyeda announced a pause in defending the rule; by March 2025 the SEC [had formally notified the Eighth Circuit](https://blogs.law.columbia.edu/climatechange/2025/07/28/uncertainty-on-climate-risk-disclosure-as-trumps-sec-abdicates-responsibility/) that it would no longer defend the climate disclosure rules; and by early 2026 the agency had indicated it intended to rescind the rules through notice-and-comment rulemaking.

The rule remains technically on the books but is stayed and unenforceable. For Diginex, the US market pivot was evident in the company's disclosed strategy: the $40 million reseller agreement with [Resulticks Global Companies Pte Limited](https://ir.diginex.com/news-releases/news-release-details/diginex-limited-nasdaq-dgnx-secures-transformative-reseller) — signed February 2026 and targeting enterprise clients in the United States, Southeast Asia, India, and the Middle East — did not anchor its pitch around SEC compliance. Instead it emphasised investor-driven ESG demand, procurement requirements, and the European and Asian regulatory ecosystems as the pull factors for US-based multinationals with global supply chains.

---

## Supply Chain: diginexLUMEN and diginexAPPRISE

The supply-chain segment represents Diginex's deepest product differentiation. DiginexLUMEN — a SaaS supply-chain due diligence platform co-developed with The Coca-Cola Company and Reckitt as anchor development partners at launch in March 2022, and later expanded to include [Unilever](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/03/31/3052183/0/en/) — provides supplier onboarding, cascading multi-tier due diligence questionnaires, algorithmic risk scoring, portfolio benchmarking against CSRD and CSDDD frameworks, and audit-ready data management. The [Forvis Mazars alliance](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/03/31/3052183/0/en/) announced in March 2025 extended distribution into the accounting firm's 100-country client base, with a specific emphasis on supply-chain climate and social risk assessment.

DiginexAPPRISE addresses labour compliance through a different entry point: multilingual, audio-based worker-voice surveys conducted in workers' native languages across 70 countries and 43 languages, with more than 600,000 worker interviews collected as of the frozen snapshot date. Decathlon and Li & Fung — a global supply-chain manager — are named reference clients. The December 2025 acquisition of The Remedy Project Limited, founded by Archana Kotecha and headquartered in Hong Kong, deepened the remediation capability that transforms worker-voice data into actionable improvement protocols, an integration directly relevant to the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive's requirements on human rights and environmental due diligence.

The regulatory tailwind for supply-chain products is structurally durable in ways that the main ESG-reporting market is not: CSRD's value-chain scope, CSDDD's due-diligence obligations, the German Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz, and analogous frameworks across Asia-Pacific create demand from both reporting companies that need supply-chain data and suppliers themselves that need to demonstrate compliance. The [SGS alliance](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/08/27/3140023/0/en/) — originally contracted in January 2022 and extended in August 2025 to include blockchain-enabled ESG data assurance — gives LUMEN-generated data a third-party assurance layer that enterprise procurement officers require before accepting supplier disclosures as credible.

---

## Revenue and the Conversion Thesis

Against this regulatory architecture, Diginex's [FY2025 results](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/diginex-limited-reports-57-revenue-increase-and-strategic-acquisitions-fiscal-year-2025) — fiscal year ending 31 March 2025 — showed the first visible step-change in SaaS conversion. Revenue reached $2.04 million, a 57 per cent increase from $1.30 million in FY2024, driven by software subscription and licence-fee growth. Gross margin remained close to 100 per cent throughout, consistent with a pure SaaS delivery model.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Operating Loss |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 (ended Mar 2022) | $1.12M | $(7.36M) |
| FY2023 (ended Mar 2023) | $1.63M | $(7.27M) |
| FY2024 (ended Mar 2024) | $1.30M | $(8.06M) |
| FY2025 (ended Mar 2025) | $2.04M | $(8.30M) |

The operating loss remained stable at roughly $8 million per annum, reflecting a deliberate choice to hold product and commercial investment constant while the regulatory triggers that would force corporate procurement decisions moved closer to execution. The $40 million Resulticks reseller agreement — structured over four years and targeting enterprise clients in markets where ISSB adoption is now mandatory or imminent — would represent the first test of whether the partnership distribution model can translate regulatory inevitability into recurring SaaS revenue at a rate that closes the gap between a $2 million top line and a self-sustaining operating profile.

chapters.title: Where DGXX sits against Workiva, Sphera, Persefoni, OneTrust, Watershed, Cority
chapters.body:
## A Crowded Market With One Clear Outlier

The ESG SaaS landscape that Diginex Limited navigated through 2024–2026 was not a level playing field. On one side sat Workiva, a publicly traded US reporting platform that had by then institutionalised itself as the de facto compliance backbone for Fortune 500 sustainability disclosures. On the other sat a cluster of well-capitalised private competitors — Sphera, Persefoni, OneTrust, Watershed, and Cority — each carrying venture or private-equity backing that dwarfed Diginex's entire market capitalisation. Against this field, Diginex's strategic logic was not to challenge the incumbents on their home turf but to anchor itself in the one geography most of them had systematically underinvested in: Asia-Pacific, where HKEX and SGX disclosure mandates were accelerating on a timeline that predated CSRD by roughly a year in practical implementation terms.

## The Workiva Benchmark

Workiva (NYSE: WK) provided the most instructive comparison because it was the only major competitor whose financials were publicly auditable against Diginex's own EDGAR filings. By fiscal year 2023, Workiva had reported subscription and support revenue of approximately $507 million against total revenues of $591 million, growing at roughly 20 percent year-over-year, with a market capitalisation that oscillated between $4.5 billion and $6 billion through 2024. Its ESG and sustainability reporting module — marketed under the connected-reporting platform brand — had by that point become a central upsell motion into its existing financial-reporting customer base, leveraging pre-built integrations with the SEC's EDGAR submission infrastructure and, increasingly, CSRD-aligned XBRL tagging.

The scale differential was stark.

| Metric | Workiva (FY2023) | Diginex (est. FY2024) |
|---|---|---|
| Total revenue | ~$591 M | Low single-digit $M |
| Subscription ARR | ~$507 M | Undisclosed / early-stage |
| Market capitalisation | ~$4.5–6 B | ~$20–50 M (NASDAQ micro-cap) |
| Primary geography | US / Europe | Asia-Pacific / Europe |
| CSRD tooling | Yes (module) | Yes (core product) |
| ISSB S1/S2 tooling | Yes | Yes |
| HKEX / SGX native support | Limited | Yes |
